transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-07
Start: 15:00 EST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (CTO - CranePort), Benji Kim (Head of ML), Jordan Reyes (Infra Lead), Aisha Grant (PM)

Auto-generated summary (may be incomplete):
Redwood overview of quickstart and hosting options, customer constraints around data residency and sensitive PII, ask for credits for a small PLG sprint and a short benchmark. Action items captured.

00:00 - 00:22 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you carving time this afternoon. I'm Maya, account exec at Redwood Inference — with me is Ravi our solutions engineer.

00:23 - 00:48 Sofia Alvarez: Hi Maya, hi Ravi, thanks. Quick intros from our side, I'm Sofia, CTO at CranePort, we run routing and ETA prediction for freight and some sensitive manifests so privacy is huge for us.

00:49 - 01:07 Benji Kim: Benji here, lead ML, we own the models and the inference stack. We are evaluating options to get something live quickly, ideally with self-serve credits so product teams can prototype.

01:08 - 01:36 Maya Chen: Perfect, that's exactly what we help with. Today I'd like to understand your TTFT targets — time to first token, the workloads and constraints — then we'll map to Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private and what a 2-week pilot could look like.

01:37 - 02:05 Jordan Reyes: For TTFT we care about two numbers: cold-start latency and steady-state p95 under our expected QPS. For prototype, low latency is nice but we can tolerate up to 600ms p95; for production it's tighter. Also we need VPC connectivity for some flows.

02:06 - 02:45 Ravi Patel: Got it. Two parts: quickstart for PLG with free credits (hosted) to validate product-market fit and then a pilot for more sensitive traffic — that might be Dedicated or a Private VPC depending on your security and latency needs. For hosted we can spin up keys and credits in minutes.

02:46 - 03:12 Sofia Alvarez: A couple specific security asks: SOC2 attestation, SSO integration (SAML/Okta), audit logs/retention, and customer-managed KMS/HSM if we go private. Is all that available?

03:13 - 03:35 Maya Chen: Yes, we have SOC2 and can do SAML SSO. For Private deployments we support KMS integrations and bring-your-own key options. Audit logs are available in Redwood Console and we can increase retention for Enterprise plans. I'll attach the security-pack.pdf after this call.

03:36 - 04:05 Benji Kim: On the ML side, we need to understand model quantization and memory footprint — do you run FP16/INT8? How do you handle KV cache across requests — we have long context dialogs for support ticket synthesis.

04:06 - 04:42 Ravi Patel: We support multiple quantization profiles; our runtime does INT8-friendly paths and picks kernels per hardware. KV cache is preserved per session and we can do prefix caching. For long contexts we often recommend a combination of prompt-chunking and KV reuse; we'll share a suggested profile in benchmark-sheet.csv.

04:43 - 05:09 Aisha Grant: For the PLG quickstart, what's the usual TTFT to a working demo — like local dev -> calling Redwood API -> first successful response? We're trying to plan an internal demo next week.

05:10 - 05:40 Maya Chen: For a simple generation flow, self-serve hosted with free credits: you can get API keys, deploy a model from the catalog, and make your first request within an hour. Typical time-to-first-token for a generated response depends on model and payload, but teams hit a demo in under a day.

05:41 - 06:25 Sofia Alvarez: That fast — great. But for PII flows we'd rather not hit hosted unless we have encryption in flight and at rest enforced. Do hosted instances support customer-side encryption or is that only private?

06:26 - 07:00 Ravi Patel: Hosted encrypts in transit and at rest by default and is SOC2 compliant for most enterprise uses, but if you require customer-managed keys or strict on-prem controls, Private/VPC or Dedicated with KMS is the move. We'll map that to your compliance checklist once you share it.

07:01 - 07:45 Benji Kim: Are there any cold-start concerns with Dedicated? We want predictable p95 when traffic ramps — sometimes dedicated pools can be scaled wrong.

07:46 - 08:20 Maya Chen: Dedicated uses reserved GPU pools with configurable autoscaling and can be tuned for concurrency and batch size. We typically set a warm pool for production rollouts. For the pilot we can recommend a small reserved config to meet your steady-state SLOs without huge commitment.

08:21 - 09:05 Jordan Reyes: Network egress policies matter — if we use VPC peering, will we be able to restrict outbound traffic and also have internal IPs only?

09:06 - 09:45 Ravi Patel: With Private VPC, you control the network config; Redwood's private dataplane sits in your VPC so egress is under your control. We'll send a network-runbook sample.

09:46 - 12:10 [Background cross talk, intermittent interruptions]

12:11 - 12:48 Sofia Alvarez: Let's talk pricing quickly — free credits are obvious for prototyping, but what's the bridge to Dedicated? Do you have trial rates or pilot discounts?

12:49 - 13:30 Maya Chen: For PLG we provide free credits to let product teams prototype. For pilots that want performance guarantees we usually propose a short-term reserved capacity with pilot pricing — not full reserved commitment, more like a trial bump to dedicated capacity. AE will share typical pilot cost ranges after we understand the expected throughput and model choice.

13:31 - 15:05 Benji Kim: From our side we'll probably start with a small LLM for routing prompts, then try a larger model for manifest abstraction. We need help picking candidate model versions that balance latency and cost.

15:06 - 15:42 Ravi Patel: We'll recommend model variants and quantization — usually start with an optimized open model we verify in the Redwood catalog; if you need lower latency, the suggestions include INT8 quantized variants or smaller family models. I'll attach the model recommendation table.

15:43 - 17:30 Aisha Grant: About telemetry — what observability will engineering have? We need per-route token usage, per-request latency histograms, and traces to link with our Sentry/Datadog.

17:31 - 18:05 Maya Chen: Redwood Console exposes per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdown, and we provide tracing hooks; integration with Datadog and Sentry is possible via webhooks or OTLP.

18:06 - 19:12 Jordan Reyes: Legal and procurement — what's typical timeline to sign an MSA for Private? Procurement will want indemnity language and DPA.

19:13 - 19:55 Maya Chen: For Private deployments we move to an enterprise contract—MSA + DPA. Timeline depends, but many customers complete legal within 4–8 weeks; we'll surface our standard templates for review.

19:56 - 22:00 Benji Kim: For the benchmark pilot, can you run with our sample payloads against hosted first to get baseline numbers? If hosted is within ~10% of dedicated latencies perhaps we can keep hosted for initial production.

22:01 - 23:10 Ravi Patel: Yes, we can run a hosted baseline with your payloads under the free credit pilot. We'll also run a dedicated emulation to estimate the delta—I'll need the payloads and concurrency pattern.

23:11 - 25:00 Sofia Alvarez: We'll share an anonymized sample set; privacy team will scrub manifests. Also, we need to validate audit log retention and export for compliance — can we export raw logs for archiving?

25:01 - 26:20 Maya Chen: You can export logs from the Console; for Private we can set up direct S3 delivery of audit logs. For hosted we have retention tiers and export endpoints.

26:21 - 30:00 [Discussion about acceptance criteria — rough notes captured verbally]

30:01 - 30:40 Benji Kim: Proposed acceptance criteria: baseline p95 under 600ms for prototype, correct redaction of PII in outputs, end-to-end encryption and audit log capture, and a simple A/B test with fallback to smaller model if latency spikes.

30:41 - 32:10 Maya Chen: That sounds reasonable. We'll map those to test steps for the pilot and document pass/fail checks.

32:11 - 35:05 Aisha Grant: Operationally, who will be our Redwood contact during the pilot? We want an SE for troubleshooting and an AE for billing/questions.

35:06 - 36:00 Maya Chen: That's us — Ravi will be the SE single point of contact for the pilot, and I'll handle billing and escalation.

36:01 - 38:15 [Brief pause while attendees check calendars]

38:16 - 42:00 Sofia Alvarez: Quick question on model rollouts — if we later want canary deploys across regions, does Redwood support A/B and automatic fallback?

42:01 - 43:12 Ravi Patel: Yes, Redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B experiments, and automatic fallback to a compatible model variant if a deployment fails. All managed via the Console rollout UI or API.

43:13 - 44:30 Benji Kim: Any gotchas we should be aware of for long-context KV caching about cost — because we prewarm caches and keep sessions which can increase token accounting?

44:31 - 45:20 Maya Chen: Token accounting is per output token; KV cache reduces compute but doesn't directly reduce token billing. We can advise on caching strategy to minimize cost while preserving latency.

45:21 - 46:12 Sofia Alvarez: Okay great. Next steps and recap?

46:13 - 47:20 Maya Chen: Recap: we'll send security-pack.pdf and SOC2 attestation (Maya). Ravi will share benchmark-sheet.csv and model recommendations and propose pilot config. CranePort will provide scrubbed sample payloads and acceptance criteria. We'll schedule a pilot kickoff week of 12/14.

47:21 - 47:55 Sofia Alvarez: Sounds good, thanks everyone. Looking forward to the security docs and bench results.

47:56 - 48:00 Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up via email with links and next steps.

References mentioned: security-pack.pdf (attached post-call), benchmark-sheet.csv (SE deliverable), model-recs.xlsx (model suggestions).

End of transcript.
